Is using AI solely for productivity missing the point?\
\
Productivity is the top priority for CEOs this year, according to a global study, and AI is often their solve. But for some founders, efficiency is just the starting point.\
\
Creative director Petter Rudwall spent a few years working with LLMs without getting a single novel idea out of them, so he built code modules that get AI models “high.” An early user of this model ran a client presentation past “altered Claude.” The famously user-flattering model told him he was playing it too safe and that his ideas weren’t interesting…and he ended up changing half of the presentation.\
\
At Meadow Memorials, a network of funeral homes, AI handles the regulatory paperwork so staff can spend more time with grieving families. As writer Sage Lazzaro frames it, it’s an efficiency, but one driven by care, not output.\
\
Which raises a bigger question: what do we actually mean by productivity? It depends on who you ask.\
\
“There’s this other presumption that we all agree [on] what productivity means… But we’re not on the same page,” says Vernon Richards, engineering manager at @phrase_platform.\
\

A contemporary republication of John B. Geijsbeek’s 1914 English translation of Luca Pacioli’s landmark 1494 treatise on bookkeeping. Redesigned and newly typeset at the exact dimensions of the original 1914 edition, the book brings the translation together with original pages, diagrams and historical material in a new editorial structure.\

Istanbul is famous for its outsized cat population who you’ll find roaming free, keeping watch, and mingling with the humans. Meet the cats who rule the city.\
\
By breakfast, the cats are already making the rounds. In Istanbul, they turn up in cafés, markets, bookstores, waterfronts and anywhere people gather.\
\
Istanbul’s official visitor guide gives cats top billing and calls them the “Royalty of Istanbul.”\
\
Istanbul’s cats are independent by design. Most don’t belong to one person, and they’re perfectly happy picking their own lookout points, routes and favorite corners.\
\
Istanbul is often cited as home to one of the largest concentrated street-cat populations in the world.\
\
If there’s a spot to claim, a cat has probably claimed it first. What’s ours is theirs.\
\
Istanbul’s cats are professional photobombers. They show up in wedding photos, tourist’s shots, and plenty of camera rolls they weren’t invited into.\
\
Istanbul helps take care of its street cats with veterinary care, vaccinations and dedicated “paw parks” where animals have space to play. Resist the urge to scoop one up and take it with you. Some have entire neighborhoods looking after them.\
\
An entire film was made about the cats of Istanbul. According to the director, “The real soul of the city is actually, I think, the cats.”\
\
Why are they so comfortable here? Because they’ve been here for centuries. They arrived on trading ships as far back as Byzantium, originally brought in to control pesky critters in cargo holds.
Ferries, trams, cats, the sea, and then the call to prayer rising over it all, and for a moment everything pauses. This is your sign to visit Istanbul.

The two continents of Istanbul meet at the water, where the city is always in motion between Europe and Asia. Follow the ferries between antique shops, family recipes, and the perfect afternoon coffee. Make your way to the best of Istanbul with a few tips from the people who know it best.\
\
For more than 20 years, Özge has lived in Istanbul cooking recipes passed down through generations. Her view of the city starts at her neighborhood market and stretches well beyond the kitchen, to antique shops, döner counters, and cafés across Europe and Asia.\
\
Çukurcuma is one of Beyoğlu’s best-known areas for antiques, with dealers, galleries and cafés lining the side streets. It’s one of the European side’s go-to neighborhoods for browsing.\
\
A La Turca is a four-story home turned antique shop. It grew out of a collectors personal collection, which is why the shop feels more curated than conventional.\
\
A La Turca house\
\
The best büfe-style döner is tucked just behind the Grand Bazaar. Kasım works the spit at Dönerci Hacı Osman’ın Yeri, where there’s a daily line until the food runs out. He keeps it moving and may even hand you a taste while you wait.\
\
The seasoned lamb is the star, piled with whole sweet peppers, freshly cut tomatoes and pickles. Get it on a plate, in pita or in their soft bread; there’s only one meat to choose from, so all you have to decide is the size.\
\
The Galata Bridge crosses the Golden Horn between the Old City and Beyoğlu. Walk across with the fishermen lining the rails while ferries pass underneath, and you get one of the best views of the Old City.\
\
From the European side, the ferry crosses the Bosphorus to Kadıköy in Asia. Grab a seat outside and watch Istanbul on both sides of the water.\
\
In Kadıköy, head to Yeldeğirmeni for street art and independent cafés. Slow down and soak it all in at Ikarus Coffee House, known for serious coffee and easy living-room vibe. \
\

If you chase after money, it has a funny way of avoiding you.\
\
At least, that's what I've found in my career.\
\
Instead, I'd much rather focus on something better:\
\
Big, painful, miserable problems.\
\
I started learning how to solve these problems back in 2009 in my startup days, and quickly figured out how valuable that was.\
\
Solve one painful problem? Here's some money.\
Solve another one? Here's more.\
Keep solving them? Here's a boatload.\
\
When you can save people money or time (or both) AND help them sleep better at night, you have incredible earning potential.\
\
So work on that skill ferociously.\
\
Here's how I do it:\
\
1. Hypothesize\
\
When you see a big problem, try to write down every single reason you think it might be happening. Guess. Jot every single thing you can think of.\
\
2. Rank\
\
Stack rank them from most likely to least likely to be the culprit. Start by cutting everything except the top 2 or 3.\
\
3. Isolate\
\
Starting with your most likely, figure out how to isolate your hypothesis and measure it effectively.\
\
4. Prove or disprove\
\
Don't guide the data. Let the data guide you. Were you right? Wrong? Talk to people as well. Qualitative and quantitative feedback are useful.\
\
5. Install\
\
Once you've figured out the actual fix, install it. Then move on to the next problem.\
\
Congrats...you're on your way to being hyper valuable.\

The worst thing in the world is getting fired without a backup plan.\
\
I've watched it happen to so many good people.\
\
$200,000 take-home pay one day.\
$0 the next day.\
\
What a nightmare.\
\
That's why planning for the worst, while working hard to prevent it, is a great 1-2 punch.\
\
Here's what I'd recommend:\
\
1. Make some noise\
\
Get online daily and share how you think about your industry. Let people see your name and face and become synonymous with something.\
\
2. Build a network\
\
Once you've made a little noise, jump into DMs. Invite people to connect. Grab coffee. Meet on Zoom. Help people. It's all about who you know.\
\
3. Show off your expertise\
\
At some point, don't just make noise. Translate noise into value. What have you helped your company accomplish? Toot your own horn.\
\
4. Collect testimonials\
\
If colleagues, managers, and peers like your work, ask them to write a little something about it. Put it on LinkedIn. Put it on your website. Show off what other people think about you.\
\
5. Connect people\
\
Lastly, make mutually beneficial connections.\
\
Once people feel like you've helped them out, they'll remember you when opportunities show up.\
\
If you can do these five things, you'll have one hell of a backup plan.\
\
Because now you're building assets that belong to you instead of your employer:\
\
A reputation.\
A network.\
Your expertise.\
Ability to create opportunities.\
\
Do that long enough and you can probably earn extra money without depending entirely on one company.\
